title: Design Patterns: Creational (Singleton, Factory, Builder, Prototype)
relevance: High — LLD / machine-coding rounds ask you to name and apply these when creating objects (parking lot vehicle types, notification channels, HTTP clients, game entities); Singleton + Factory come up most at campus; Builder/Prototype at mid-level product cos.
company_notes: Campus/new-grad LLD and machine coding (India product cos, FAANG new-grad): Factory (simple or method) and Singleton are nearly mandatory; Builder when entities have many optional attributes; Prototype less often unless games/templates. Experienced/SDE-2 LLD: precise Factory Method vs Abstract Factory, thread-safe Singleton tradeoffs, choosing not to Singleton everything, fluent Builder for request/query objects. Creational patterns are the first pattern family probed and show up inside almost every canonical LLD problem as how you create X.

phases.goal: Establish what creational patterns are for and when to reach for each one in an interview.

must_hit.point: Creational patterns control how objects are created so clients depend on abstractions rather than scattering new ConcreteX() everywhere.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says construction logic is centralized/flexible and clients program to interfaces, not concrete classes.

must_hit.point: Singleton means one instance with global access via a private constructor and static getInstance; prefer DI/shared instance unless the domain truly needs a process-wide single resource.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names private ctor + getInstance and gives logger/config/connection pool as the rare justified cases.

must_hit.point: Interview pick order: simple factory/Factory Method when type varies at runtime; Builder when configuration is complex; Abstract Factory when families must match; Prototype when copy-from-template beats rebuild; Singleton last and only when truly global.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks the decision order without stacking every pattern by default.

probes: What problem do creational patterns solve, and how would you choose among Factory, Builder, Abstract Factory, Prototype, and Singleton in an LLD round?

hints.1: Think about what varies: the concrete type, the configuration knobs, a matching family, or an expensive template.
hints.2: Start from runtime type variation → complex optional config → consistent product families → clone-from-template → only then a true process-wide single instance.
hints.3: Simple factory/Factory Method for type; Builder for config; Abstract Factory for families; Prototype for copy-from-template; Singleton last only if truly global.

phases.goal: Show how each major creational pattern is structured and how the common interview variants work.

must_hit.point: Thread-safe Singleton checklist in Java: naive lazy is broken under races; then synchronized getInstance; then double-checked locking with volatile; then Bill Pugh static holder; enum Singleton is serialization/reflection-safe; eager init is fine if always needed.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Can sketch the progression and name enum or Bill Pugh as the strong Java answers.

must_hit.point: Simple factory (not GoF) is one class/method with if/switch returning a product interface; Factory Method has Creator declare createProduct() and ConcreteCreators override to return ConcreteProducts so new types are added via subclasses (OCP).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts conditional one-class factory with polymorphic creators and Product interface use by clients.

must_hit.point: Abstract Factory creates a family of related products that must stay consistent together; Builder does step-by-step construction for many optional fields (fluent withX().build(), optional Director for named recipes); Prototype creates by cloning via clone()/copy(), with registries returning clones never the live prototype.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives family consistency for Abstract Factory, telescoping-constructor pain for Builder, and clone/registry for Prototype.

probes: Walk through Factory Method versus a simple factory, then explain how Abstract Factory, Builder, and Prototype each structure object creation.

hints.1: Separate “one place with conditionals” from “subclass chooses the product.”
hints.2: For Abstract Factory talk families; for Builder talk optional fields and build(); for Prototype talk clone and registry.
hints.3: Simple factory = if/switch; Factory Method = Creator/createProduct overrides; Abstract Factory = matching family; Builder = fluent steps + optional Director; Prototype = clone, registry never hands out the live prototype.

phases.goal: Judge when each pattern helps versus when it is overkill or harmful.

must_hit.point: Singleton is hard to mock, violates SRP, and needs concurrency care; production often prefers an injected shared instance over a true Singleton.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States testability/global-state cost and offers DI as the alternative.

must_hit.point: Abstract Factory is overkill if you only ever create one product type; Factory Method or simple factory is enough—families are the trigger.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Refuses Abstract Factory for a single varying interface and reserves it for coordinated product sets.

must_hit.point: Builder plus private constructor can enforce invariants at build() and yield an immutable product; setters allow half-built mutable objects.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts incomplete mutable setter objects with a build()-gated immutable result.

probes: When would you reject Singleton or Abstract Factory, and why prefer Builder over setters for a complex object?

hints.1: Ask whether you truly need global uniqueness or a whole matching family.
hints.2: Singleton costs SRP/testability; Abstract Factory needs multiple related product types; Builder’s win is invariants at build time.
hints.3: Prefer injected shared instance over Singleton; skip Abstract Factory for one product type; Builder+private ctor beats setters for immutability and invariants.

phases.goal: Map creational patterns onto typical LLD prompts and attack drills interviewers use.

must_hit.point: Pattern mapping drills: notification Email/SMS/Push → factory; HTTP request with 8 optional fields → Builder; light/dark UI widget set → Abstract Factory; spawn 100 similarly configured enemies → Prototype; app-wide logger → Singleton.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Assigns each prompt to one pattern with a one-sentence justification.

must_hit.point: Factory Method vs Abstract Factory drill: PaymentProcessor factory for card/UPI/wallet, then when each channel needs matching ReceiptFormatter and FraudChecker, refactor to Abstract Factory because mixing families is wrong.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows single-product factory first, then family consistency as the reason to upgrade.

must_hit.point: Prototype shallow vs deep: an object with List inventory shows why shallow clone corrupts both copies when one mutates the list; deep-copy fixes it; optional registry keyed by enemy type.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains shared mutable list under shallow copy and how deep copy/registry clones isolate instances.

probes: For notifications, an HTTP request with many optional fields, a themed UI widget set, many similar enemies, and a logger—which creational pattern fits each and why?

hints.1: Match each scenario to what varies: type, optional config, family consistency, clone-from-template, or global instance.
hints.2: Factory for channel types; Builder for optional HTTP fields; Abstract Factory for matching UI families; Prototype for similar enemies; Singleton only for the logger case.
hints.3: Email/SMS/Push = factory; 8-field HTTP request = Builder; light/dark widgets = Abstract Factory; 100 enemies = Prototype; app-wide logger = Singleton.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Simple factory is one class with conditionals returning a product interface; Factory Method uses polymorphic creators so types extend via new subclasses (OCP). Most campus answers use simple factory and that is OK if named honestly; interviewers often say factory and mean the simple form.

Factory Method varies one product type through Creator subclasses. Abstract Factory is a factory of related factories for a consistent family (e.g., Button+Checkbox for a theme/OS). Use Abstract Factory only when products must stay consistent together; it is overkill for a single varying type.

Singleton gives one instance and global access but is hard to mock, violates SRP, and needs concurrency care. Prefer DI/shared instance passed in unless the domain truly needs a process-wide resource (logger, config, connection pool). In toy LLD a Logger Singleton is common; in production prefer injected shared instance and call out the testability cost.

Builder replaces telescoping constructors for complex objects with many optional fields; fluent withX().build() is interview-friendly and an optional Director encodes named recipes. Setters allow half-built mutable objects; Builder with a private constructor can enforce invariants at build() and yield an immutable product.

tradeoffs.topic: Prototype clone vs external new + copy fields
tradeoffs.strong_answer: External copy breaks encapsulation of private fields and couples to concrete classes; clone()/copy() keeps copying inside the type hierarchy. Always distinguish shallow vs deep copy; registries should return clones, never the live prototype.
Factory Method often evolves into Abstract Factory, Builder, or Prototype; Abstract Factories, Builders, and Prototypes can themselves be Singletons—but do not stack patterns without a reason.

gotchas.trap: Treating a static create() method as a Factory Method
gotchas.correction: No—static creation methods cannot be overridden; Factory Method relies on subclassing. See the Factory Comparison distinction among creation method, simple factory, Factory Method, and Abstract Factory.

gotchas.trap: Defaulting the Logger to a Singleton without discussion
gotchas.correction: Often yes in toy LLD; in production prefer an injected shared instance. Interview win is acknowledging testability and global-state cost.

gotchas.trap: Confusing simple factory with Factory Method
gotchas.correction: Simple factory = one class with conditionals; Factory Method = polymorphic creators. Campus answers using simple factory are fine if named honestly.

gotchas.trap: Reaching for Abstract Factory when only one product type varies
gotchas.correction: If you only ever create one product type (one interface), Factory Method or simple factory is enough; families are the trigger.

gotchas.trap: Using setters instead of Builder for complex construction
gotchas.correction: Setters allow half-built mutable objects; Builder plus private constructor can enforce invariants at build() and yield an immutable product.

gotchas.trap: Prototype via external field copying, or ignoring shallow vs deep
gotchas.correction: External copy breaks encapsulation and couples to concrete classes; clone() keeps copying in the type hierarchy. Always ask shallow vs deep—e.g., a shared List inventory means shallow clone corrupts both copies on mutation.
